key_insight: In this study, psychological comorbidities—especially depression and anxiety—were more strongly associated with chronic low back pain than MRI-defined spine abnormalities.
clinical_relevance: For infographic use, the main message is that chronic low back pain may reflect a biopsychosocial condition more than a purely structural spine problem.
method: Retrospective study of 1,480 patients with lumbar spine MRI from a Chicago health system (2014–2024).
GPT-4 was used to extract spinal pathologies from radiology reports and was compared with a rule-based regex pipeline.
Multivariable and leave-one-domain-out regression models assessed how demographic, socioeconomic, psychological, and anatomical factors related to cLBP.
evidence_signal: The LLM extraction pipeline achieved F1=0.98 versus 0.92 for regex, and psychological factors produced the largest model impact (ΔAIC=120.1).
watch_item: This is an observational, single-region retrospective study, so associations do not prove causation and may not generalize across settings or populations.
paper_title: Psychological factors contribute more to chronic low back pain than spine pathology: An LLM-based analysis of radiology reports
